answer: The terms put everything that isn't MySQL, Postgres or Oracle under one blanket (like sorting people into 'technical' and 'non-technical', unfair to the second group) and hide real differences; most of these databases were built for very specific problems, so name the specific type. 'NoSQL databases scale' is wrong as a blanket statement: you can build a non-relational database that doesn't scale at all, and the ones that scale (Cassandra, MongoDB, DynamoDB) scale for a very specific workload.
evidence: §1.1 Name the database, not the family: 'puts everything that isn't MySQL, Postgres or Oracle under one blanket... As a blanket statement it is wrong. You can build a non-relational database that doesn't scale at all... Cassandra scales, but for a very specific workload.'

answer: As a very broad separation, not always true: they typically give up consistency (strong/CAP consistency) to give you scalability, and availability: with multiple nodes the system scales horizontally and stays highly available.
evidence: §1.2: 'non-relational databases typically give up consistency to give you scalability'; board: 'In most cases, NoSQL databases provide scalability and availability by compromising consistency.'

answer: ACID consistency: data correctness, every transaction moves the database from one correct state to another. CAP consistency: visibility, once you write data it is available to query right away (strong consistency; precisely, linearizability). NoSQL databases give up the CAP one. A database can be ACID and still not linearizable.
evidence: §1.2 Two meanings of consistency: 'Consistency in ACID is about the data being correct... Consistency in the CAP theorem is about visibility... That is strong consistency, and it is the consistency non-relational databases give up.'

answer: Relational databases wanted all data in one place, in one database instance; if that instance goes down the whole system is down, so it is not highly available (in practice standby replicas can take over; PostgreSQL streaming replication is async by default and can lose commits). Non-relational ones spread data horizontally so other nodes still serve if one fails, almost never complete downtime. The price: they become eventually consistent (a write shows up everywhere but not at once). Exceptions exist since nothing is standardised, e.g. DynamoDB: eventually consistent by default, ConsistentRead=true returns latest data at twice the read cost; GSI reads always eventual.
evidence: §1.2: 'Relational databases wanted all the data in one place, in one database instance. If that instance goes down, the system is down... They become eventually consistent... DynamoDB is a good example of an exception.'

answer: 'NoSQL DBs scale does not mean SQL does not → anything that shards, scales.' Backed by Lecture 03's key-value store on MySQL sharded by key range: keys A–M on one database, N–Z on another, giving an almost highly available, horizontally scalable system at the cost of (cross-shard) consistency. (The page also cites Vitess sharding MySQL for YouTube.)
evidence: §1.3 Relational databases scale too: 'The class board boxed it: NoSQL DBs scale does not mean SQL does not → anything that shards, scales... In Lecture 03 the key-value store on MySQL was split across databases: one held the keys from A to M, the other the keys from N to Z.'

answer: Properties: mostly JSON-based (no hard rule); support complex queries (aggregations in MongoDB, faceted queries in Elasticsearch); you can query on the attributes of a document; and partial updates (update one attribute in a document). Examples: MongoDB and Elasticsearch.
evidence: §2.1 Document databases: 'The famous examples are MongoDB and Elasticsearch. They are mostly JSON-based... They support complex queries... you can query on the attributes of a document... you can make partial updates.'

answer: A document database, because it gives almost the features the relational database gave (close to relational in power). A key-value store is far more restrictive (only key-wise access, no querying inside values), so teams almost never jump straight to one.
evidence: §2.1: 'when a team moves a generic relational schema off SQL, it typically adopts a document database, because that gives it almost the features the relational database gave. You will almost never see a team jump straight to a key-value store.'

answer: Partial update: update just one attribute of a document in place (e.g. $set settings.tz), nothing else touched. In a key-value store the value is an opaque blob, so you must read the whole value, update it yourself, and write the whole value back (exception: Redis hashes allow HSET on one field).
evidence: §2.1 and §2.3: 'in this document, update just this one attribute'; 'The value is a blob. If you want to update it, you read it, update it and write it back. No partial update is possible... Redis hashes let HSET set individual fields.'

answer: DynamoDB is a key-value store, not a document database, yet it lets you query within the document (supports both key-value and document models). So focus on the access pattern and the features you want (complex queries, partial updates, etc.) and which database gives them, not the category label.
evidence: §2.2 The lines are blurry: 'DynamoDB is a key-value store, not a document database, yet it still lets you query within the document... understand the access pattern and the features... What you need to know as an engineer is which features you want from a database and which database gives you them.'

answer: MongoDB: it started out saying 'we are BASE, not ACID', and is now ACID compliant (maybe not as optimally as the SQL world).
evidence: §2.2: 'MongoDB is the example. It started out saying we are BASE, not ACID. Now MongoDB is ACID compliant, maybe not as optimally as the SQL world, but compliant.'

answer: Only key-wise operations: get a key, put a key, delete a key, insert a key, insert a value into the set at a key (GET, PUT, DEL, SET, SADD); you never peek into the value. Examples: Redis, DynamoDB and Aerospike.
evidence: §2.3: 'Examples are Redis, DynamoDB and Aerospike... Every operation you make, reads, writes, deletes, all of them, is key-wise: get a key, put a key, delete a key, insert a key, insert a value into the set at a key.'

answer: Every KV operation names exactly one key, so it lands on exactly one shard and never needs a cross-shard query; it can be partitioned into thousands of partitions without hiccups, each answering in parallel. Richer query models allow range operations and IN (e.g. id in 1,2,3 across three databases), which cross shards and must wait for all of them, which is very expensive. The more complex the queries, the less you can distribute the data.
evidence: §2.3: 'Because everything is key-wise, you can shard the database very easily: you never have to make a cross-shard query... Cross-shard queries come from range operations and the IN operator... you can partition it very heavily, thousands and thousands of partitions, without any hiccups.'

answer: You give up the power of complex queries (restricted, key-only access, no partial update), and in exchange get massive partitioning/parallelism, best performance and availability.
evidence: §2.3 table: 'What you give up... Key-value: The power of complex queries; you gain parallelism and availability'; 'by limiting access, you get massive parallelism... you pay for it with restricted access.'

answer: Row store: each row's five values (R1, R2, R3) stored next to each other as one long strip, a row's columns together. Column store: each column's values stored together (c1 symbol through c5 timestamp), so R1, R2, R3 are each one cell in every column block, the lines crossing every block.
evidence: §3.1 Fig 3·a: 'In a row store, the five values of each row, R1, R2 and R3, are stored next to each other as one long strip. In a column store, the values of each column are stored together, c1 symbol through c5 timestamp, so row 1 is one cell in every column block.'

answer: A very crude, naive picture: one separate file per column; line 1 of each file holds that column's value for row 1, line 2 for row 2, etc. (row 2 = line 2 of every file).
evidence: §3.1: 'A very crude, very naive way to picture it, and only a picture: one separate file per column. Line 1 of each file holds that column's value for row 1...'

answer: The average price of the entire stock market for one day: SELECT avg(price) WHERE ts = '...' (about 10,000 listed companies, ~10,000 entries for the date). It needs only two columns: price and timestamp.

answer: The row is the unit on disk: all columns of a row sit together, so the engine reads the entire row even if you name only two columns, then filters. It can't skip to the next row's price without passing over this row's other columns, because it must know where the row ends. On a 100-column table it goes row by row reading all columns and discarding 98 of them, wasting disk IO.
evidence: §3.2: 'Write a SELECT that names just two columns instead of a star, and the disk still reads the entire row'; board: a row database 'will go row by row reading all columns & discarding 98 of them'; 'Because the row is the unit on disk. Unless the engine knows where this row ends, it can't pick out the corresponding columns of the next one.'

answer: Only the files of the needed columns: exactly two files, price and timestamp; no disk IO at all for symbol, name and exchange (with 100 columns, still just 2 files).
evidence: §3.2: 'On a column store the same query reads exactly two files, price and timestamp. It does no disk IO at all for symbol, name and exchange.'

answer: The instructor bought Grammarly, triggered the OTP, and immediately got a call from HDFC Bank. It drives the unread count, the 'you last read until here' line, and jumping to that point when you open a channel with many new messages; also why Slack doesn't replay old messages over the socket.
evidence: §6.5 The checkpoint: 'for this user in this channel, the point up to which they have read... The unread message count. The you last read until here line. And when you click a channel with a hundred new messages, being taken to that point.'

answer: Whether they're active, how they interact with the channel, muted, favourited (no separate favourites table), notification settings — every interaction a user has with a channel, making membership the key table.
evidence: §6.2 and §6.5: 'how far this user has read, whether they're active, how they interact with the channel'; 'Muted the channel? Store it on membership. Favourited it?... Notification settings, the same.'

answer: 1) Name things as nouns (a noun gives a table a persona and room to grow). 2) Piggyback on what you already have instead of writing ifs and elses (DM as a two-person channel).
evidence: §6.5 rule: 'Name things as nouns, and piggyback on what you already have instead of writing ifs and elses. The two takeaways of the schema.'

answer: A sharded relational database (board: any DB you can shard — MySQL, Cassandra, Mongo; 'even SQL works!'). Enterprise chat doesn't have a very high message rate (people are there to work), so you just store and scroll; what's needed is sharding/partitioning (put several enterprise customers per DB), not a fancy NoSQL. Slack itself runs MySQL/Vitess.
evidence: §7.1: 'The design assumes the messages are stored in a relational database that is sharded... messages don't arrive at a very high rate... No fancy NoSQL database is needed.'

answer: Instagram Messenger: everyone is chit-chatting and all users are in one database, so he'd pick Cassandra, built for a high ingestion rate.

answer: Receiving needs the WebSocket so people don't have to refresh, but that doesn't mean sending must go over it: 'Just because you have it does not mean you have to use it.' Ask what guarantees you get or lose by sending over a WebSocket.

answer: If the WebSocket were always better, why would REST exist? And Slack isn't as frequent as Instagram Messenger — you don't receive that many messages on Slack/Teams. Its customers are enterprises, for whom a persisted message matters more than saving per-message overhead. Everything has an overhead; 'it's open' isn't reasoning. (Also HTTP/1.1 reuses persistent connections.)
evidence: §7.2: 'If the WebSocket were always better, why does REST exist at all? And is Slack really as frequent as your Instagram Messenger?... for them a message being persisted matters more than saving overhead.'

answer: A sent message first shows grey, then turns black after a visible delay — a hint, not proof, that sending isn't instant/over the WebSocket but an ordinary API call.
evidence: §7.2: 'A sent message first shows grey, then turns black. It isn't sent in an instant... That delay is one hint, not proof, that Slack most probably doesn't send messages over the WebSocket.'

answer: 1: Slack (instructor's hypothesis) — over HTTP through LB to API server, saved to sharded DB, then tells the edge server (synchronous). 2: a hypothetical WhatsApp-like app — over WebSocket to edge server, delivered at once, handed to Kafka, workers pull and save later (asynchronous). 3: Zoom chat — over WebSocket, delivered to whoever is connected, never saved (non-persistent).
evidence: §7.3 Fig 7·c: 'One, Slack in the instructor's hypothesis... Two, a hypothetical WhatsApp-like app... Three, Zoom chat.'

answer: Just a fancy name for a WebSocket server, the server holding users' WebSocket connections — not a CDN/CloudFront edge server; standard terminology. Any service needing to reach users in real time goes through the fleet.
evidence: §7.3: 'an edge server, which is just a fancy name for a WebSocket server'; §7.4: 'does not mean a CloudFront edge server.'

answer: For an enterprise app where communication is key, broadcasting before saving is a bad experience and costs credibility: people could misquote you ('I received this message, see'). Also Slack users read channels from the database on refresh, and they don't keep their own local store of messages like WhatsApp users.
evidence: §7.3 ① Slack: 'Unless it is saved, it should not be sent to anyone... It costs credibility, because people can then misquote you.' 'Slack users can refresh a channel and read its messages from the database.'

answer: Synchronous: user sends the message over HTTP to an API server; the API server persists it in the database; then the API server sends it as an event to the WebSocket (edge) server, which delivers it to users in real time. Sending over HTTP, receiving over WebSocket.
evidence: §7.3: 'The user sends the message over HTTP to an API server; the API server persists it in the database; then the API server sends the message, as an event, to the WebSocket server, which delivers it to the users in real time.'

answer: Message goes over the WebSocket to the edge server, which sends it straight to the other user in real time and pushes it onto Kafka; workers store it in the DB later, asynchronously. Acceptable because a copy already lives on the user's device and users don't read others' messages from the backend; gains: no synchronous DB call, batchable writes, real-time experience. (Thought experiment; WhatsApp doesn't store in a backend.)
evidence: §7.3 ② WhatsApp-like: 'The edge server sends it straight to the other user, in real time, and pushes it onto Kafka, from where it is stored in the database later... That is acceptable because a copy already lives on the user's device.'

answer: Slack users refresh a channel and read from the database. If the async save lags (say 10 minutes), others are notified at once, but on refresh the message is missing because the DB doesn't have it yet — a message they already saw disappears.
evidence: §7.3: 'Say the asynchronous save takes 10 minutes... They refresh the page, and the message isn't there, because the page loads from a database that doesn't have it yet.'

answer: Non-persistent: cares only about real time, not persistence. Example: Zoom (in-meeting) chat — everyone connected gets it; leave and rejoin and you don't see earlier messages (by default; continuous meeting chat can persist).
evidence: §7.3 ③ Zoom chat: 'The third type cares only about real time, not about persistence at all. Zoom chat is the classic example.'

answer: It is already handling a ton of TCP connections (extra load, risk of overwhelming it); it's open on the internet, so a DB connection string there is a security problem (credentials almost exposed; if compromised, you're gone); and if it goes down the entire real-time communication goes down. Companies keep it dumb: relay messages/events, at most push into an async queue (Kafka connection string only).
evidence: §7.4 Keep the edge server dumb: 'It is already handling a ton of TCP connections. It is open on the internet, so holding a connection string to the database there is a security problem. And if it goes down, the entire real-time communication of your platform goes down with it.'

answer: Guarantees are very slim, retries would be much higher, and the client would end up doing the broadcast instead of the server (who tells B the message is there?). A micro-optimisation saving little overhead for retry complexity and needlessly complex client code; UDP fits where dropping data is OK, not critical persistence. Keep it simple.
evidence: §7.5: 'the guarantees are very slim, the retries would be much higher, and the client would end up taking care of the broadcast instead of the server.'

answer: They offer a persistent connection, not database persistence. Getting DB persistence through the WebSocket means the WS server talks to the DB: more load, security implications, risk of overwhelming, real-time backbone breaks if it goes down.
evidence: §7.4: 'They offer a persistent connection, not database persistence, and database persistence is what matters for Slack.'

answer: At most a Kafka connection string (to put messages into Kafka) — ideally a least-privilege, write-only credential; never database credentials.
evidence: §7.4: 'At most it puts a message into Kafka, holding nothing but a Kafka connection string.' §9.4: 'write-only to one topic'.

answer: For the Slack flow (path 1): a line from the user over HTTP (through the load balancer) to the API server, from the API server to the sharded database to save, and then from the API server to the edge (WebSocket) server, which delivers to the other user.
evidence: §7.3 Fig 7·c: 'One, Slack in the instructor's hypothesis: over HTTP through a load balancer to an API server, which saves it to the sharded database and then tells the edge server to deliver it.' Labels: 'then tell the edge'.

answer: Deliberately: any implementation is possible depending on guarantees, and the lecture keeps designs conflicting and never converges on one, so you think about every decision and choose by guarantee rather than copying a diagram. The async Kafka route is possible for Slack too.
evidence: §9.2 Why Kafka: 'This diagram uses Kafka, type ②, on purpose... The lecture deliberately keeps its designs conflicting and never converges on one, so that you think about every single decision.'

answer: The features it drives through them are its most critical ones (e.g. Discord's chat, video streaming); if the WebSocket servers go down, real-time stops. An expensive TCP connection is kept open so it isn't re-established each time, giving low-latency communication and a rich experience.
evidence: §8.1: 'Whenever a company uses WebSockets, or any persistent connection, the features it drives through them are its most critical ones.'

answer: Assume a WebSocket server can hold only four connections (real ones hold far more). Channel C1 has five users A–E; A, B, C, D fill WS1, so E connects to WS2.
evidence: §8.1: 'assume the limit is four... channel 1 (C1), with five users: A, B, C, D and E... When E connects, WS1 is full, so E connects to a second server, WS2.'

answer: A server built with Socket.io or equivalent knows which users are connected through the handshake; drawn as a local connection pool inside each edge server.
evidence: §8.1: 'A WebSocket server built with Socket.io, or any equivalent library, knows which users are connected to it: the handshake tells it.'

answer: After connecting, the client sends meta information: its membership, the channels it belongs to (e.g. 'I am part of C1, C2 and C3'); the server keeps it in memory or on disk.
evidence: §8.1: 'after the connection is established, the client first sends meta information: its membership, the channels it is part of.'

answer: Whenever a user joins or leaves a channel, the information is sent to the server, and users also resend their membership periodically; the server is kept eventually consistent.
evidence: §8.1: 'Memberships change, so the server is kept eventually consistent with them. Whenever a user joins or leaves a channel, the information is sent to the server, and users also resend their membership periodically.'

answer: WS1 looks up who is in C1 (A, B, C, D), skips A as the sender, and sends to B, C and D.
evidence: §8.1: 'finds A, B, C and D, skips A because A sent it, and sends the message to B, C and D.'

answer: A messaging service slows things down, you need a bunch of consumers running, and each server would consume a lot from it. Start simple / from first principles.
evidence: §8.2: 'Why a messaging service? It slows things down, you need a bunch of consumers running, and each server would be consuming a lot from it. Start simple.'

answer: WS1 opens one normal TCP connection (not a WebSocket) to WS2 and sends the message over it; WS2 sees it's for C1, looks up its users in C1, finds E and delivers.
evidence: §8.2: 'WS1 establishes one TCP connection with WS2: a normal TCP connection, not a WebSocket connection... WS2 sees the message is for C1... finds E, and sends it to E.'

answer: WS1 built a TCP connection to WS3 as well (a second link), so A's message goes locally to B, C, D, over one link to WS2/E and the other to WS3/F.
evidence: §8.2: 'User F joins C1, but... establishes the WebSocket connection with a third server, WS3. WS1 builds a TCP connection to WS3 as well.'

answer: A server going down is a fault-tolerance problem, not the overhead in question (same for making it async to catch up). Sending to servers that don't need the message can be minimised with a global state, and even then a much bigger overhead remains (the connections). Server discovery is a different problem.
evidence: §8.3: 'a server going down is fault tolerance'; 'Every message is sent to every server... That can be minimised and optimised with a global state, and even then a much bigger overhead remains.'

answer: No. The TCP connection is established once and messages are relayed over it; not re-established per message.
evidence: §8.3: 'No: the TCP connection is established once, and messages are just relayed over it.'

answer: Each server has a limited number of connections, and in a mesh every server must hold a persistent TCP link to every other, so many of its connections are hogged for inter-server talk instead of serving users: 4 users + 3 peers = 7 connections, 3 serving no user; at 100 servers, 99 links each. (Page: the limit is file descriptors/memory/CPU, not ports.)
evidence: §8.3: 'a lot of each server's persistent TCP connections are hogged just to stay connected to the other servers. With four users connected to a server and three peer servers, it holds seven connections.'

answer: A real-time Pub/Sub (e.g. Redis, not Kafka) in the middle; each WebSocket server needs a single connection to it (WS1: 4 users + 1 link).
evidence: §8.4: 'Put a Pub/Sub in the middle instead, and every WebSocket server creates a single connection to it... reduced to just one.'

answer: It sends the message to everyone subscribed/connected right now, pushing it. It gives zero persistence, doesn't store messages, and doesn't guarantee delivery: a server not connected at that moment misses it (at-most-once).
evidence: §8.4: 'send this message to everyone who is subscribed to it right now. It gives you zero persistence... A real-time Pub/Sub does not guarantee delivery; its only guarantee is to send the message to everyone connected to it at that moment.'

answer: Both Redis Pub/Sub and Slack have 'channels' (few words to go around), so the page says Slack channel or Redis channel to avoid confusion. Broadcasting every message to all servers is wasteful; a C1 message should go only to servers with members of C1 (e.g. WS2 with E and F), not WS3/WS4.
evidence: §8.5: 'Redis Pub/Sub has channels, and Slack has channels... Broadcasting every message to all the WebSocket servers is wasteful.'

answer: The server subscribes, not the user. When a WS server spins up it connects to the Redis Pub/Sub; when a user connects and tells its membership ('I am part of channel 1'), the server fires a Redis SUBSCRIBE for that channel (also when the user joins a new channel).
evidence: §8.5: 'When a user connects to the server and tells it its membership... the server fires a Redis subscribe command and subscribes itself to that channel. It is the server that subscribes, not the user.'

answer: A sends to WS1; WS1 delivers to B, C, D; WS1 publishes to Redis channel C1; Redis pushes it to the server subscribed to C1, WS2; WS2 delivers to E and F. WS3 (G, H, subscribed only to C2) gets nothing. Pushed, not pulled.
evidence: §8.5: 'A sends a message to WS1. WS1 sends it to B, C and D. WS1 sends it to Redis Pub/Sub on channel 1. Redis sends it to... WS2, and WS2 sends it to... E and F.' Fig 8·f: 'WS3 is subscribed to c2 only and gets nothing.'

answer: No. The message is literally pushed to WS2; WS2 does not pull it.
evidence: §8.5: 'The message is literally pushed to WS2. WS2 does not pull it.'

answer: Use a cluster of Redis Pub/Sub, sharded, with intelligent balancing (note: in Redis Cluster classic PUBLISH goes to every node; sharded Pub/Sub SSUBSCRIBE/SPUBLISH since 7.0 scales). Reduce load with the Balancer putting an organisation's users on the same edge server so their messages never touch Redis (only the worst case does).
evidence: §8.5: 'Have a cluster of it, sharded, with intelligent balancing.' §8.6: 'If all the users of an organisation connect to the same server, there is no need to send their messages to Redis at all.'

evidence: §8.6: 'When a user opens the Slack app, the client talks to it and asks where do I connect?. It answers with the IP address of a WebSocket server... It is like DNS, but it is not DNS.'

evidence: §8.6: 'Naively, give each organisation its own WebSocket server. Organisations on Slack have 200, 500, 10,000 or 20,000 employees, and that is nothing for one WebSocket server.'

answer: Nothing serious. Its users ask the Balancer again and get another server's IP; the Balancer notices the server is down and moves users. For a while an org's users may be spread across servers and their messages go through Redis, which is fine; the Balancer later regroups/rebalances (even killing connections intermittently) to minimise Redis IO.
evidence: §8.6: 'What if this server goes down? Oh my God, life ended. No. Nothing serious happens. Its users talk to the Balancer again and get another server's IP address.'

answer: Any service that wants to talk to users in real time — chat, notifications or anything else — sends its information through these edge servers.
evidence: §9.1 Fig 9·a: 'every real-time service, chat or notifications, goes through them.'

Separately, a load balancer and API servers handle non-real-time requests (channel scroll, muted channels) reading the same DB. One message A→B: 1 persist in Kafka, 2 find B in local pool, 3 send to B.

answer: Both fine. Exposing directly: no extra hop but open to attacks, so harden it and keep no secrets on it (used for ultra-low latency, e.g. streaming a live class). Behind a load balancer: one more hop, about 3–5 ms per hop (instructor's estimate), connection always sticky, and the edge server can be private and call internal APIs (e.g. membership checks). If the latency is acceptable use the LB; if not, keep it public. (Slack uses Envoy proxies.)
evidence: §9.4: 'a public edge server can be attacked, and a load balancer in front of it adds one more hop, about five milliseconds... If that latency is acceptable, use the load balancer; if not, keep it public. Both are fine.'

answer: Harden it and put it through a very high security review: change the route tables, hide all ports, prevent SSH, block a lot on the machine; put no credentials on it (zero DB credentials, at most a Kafka connection string); a simple rate limiter against DDoS (page note: infra-level floods need upstream capacity).
evidence: §9.4: 'it is hardened and goes through a very high security review: you change the route tables, hide all the ports, prevent SSH... whenever a server is exposed on the internet, you don't put any credentials on it.'

answer: All you lose is the Kafka connection string; Kafka is internal so no one outside can talk to it; worst an attacker can do is a DDoS, prevented by a simple rate limiter. evidence: §9.4: 'If the server is compromised, all you lose is that string, and the Kafka is internal'; 'the worst an attacker can do is a DDoS... a simple rate limiter can prevent a DDoS.' More precisely notes.

answer: No expiration, because there is no persistence: nobody stores the message; it's received and sent on to subscribers.
evidence: §8.4: 'There is no expiration, because there is no persistence: no one stores the message anywhere.'

answer: Don't trust the client for critical membership (private channels): check membership via a backend API (or the DB) on the server side, which means making the edge server private behind a load balancer. (Instructor called it MITM; page: it's broken access control, deny by default.)

answer: Calling a service every time to find where a message goes is far too expensive and no longer real time; even with caching it's still a network call each time. Overkill when the edge server can hold the routing info itself; keep it simple.

answer: Persistence is guaranteed (messages once sent always persisted); the real-time notification/push to other users is not (Redis may lose it; user sees it on refresh).

answer: Use several Redis instances, a cluster of Redis, rather than one; plus the Balancer keeps most traffic (same org on one server) from reaching Redis at all.

answer: Kafka is pull-based (consumers pull) and persists historical messages (for a retention window); Redis Pub/Sub pushes to everyone connected and has zero persistence. Not just 'Kafka is async'. Neither superior: Redis for real time, Kafka for persistence; very contextual.

answer: No. The message goes to users immediately as a real-time notification; only storage is delayed ('Not delivered, stored'). The cost: until persisted, the source of truth lacks it, so a refresh won't show a message already seen.

answer: Store important data with standby nodes and replication factor three, done by the database's storage engine (write to one node, replicated to two others), not by workers pushing to multiple instances. The DB doesn't acknowledge/commit until written in three places (DynamoDB actually acks at 2 of 3); a write lost before that was never accepted. Not by re-reading Kafka.
evidence: §9.5: 'important data is stored with standby nodes and a replication factor of three... The worker doesn't do that; the database's storage engine does... your DB would never say that I am done unless it is written in three different places.'
